# Sequence alignment

Chapter 5 had you write down two protein lengths. Human BRCA1 is 1,863 amino
acids and mouse Brca1 is 1,812. The coding sequences behind those proteins are
5,592 and 5,439 bases, so the human one carries 153 bases the mouse one lacks.
Where are they? One block near the end would mean one thing. Thirty small
pieces scattered through the gene would mean something quite different. Nothing
you've done so far can tell those two stories apart.

## Lining two sequences up is a scoring problem

A [pairwise alignment]{.term def="Two sequences written one above the other,
gaps allowed, so every column holds one base from each or a base against a
gap."} is what you get when you write two sequences one above the other and
allow yourself to push gaps into either one. The format has no other rules.

There are a great many ways to do it, and no program tries them all. None has
to. The highest-scoring one can be computed directly, one column at a time,
without the others ever being written down.

Best by what standard, though? No output anywhere answers that, and it's the
point of this chapter. You hand the program four numbers and it returns the
arrangement with the highest total. It has no other definition of a good
alignment, and it has no access to what actually happened to these two genes.

The smallest example that shows it uses two made-up sequences, seven bases
against five, so any global alignment of them needs two gap columns.

```{python}
from Bio.Align import PairwiseAligner

toy_aligner = PairwiseAligner(mode="global")
toy_aligner.match_score = 1
toy_aligner.mismatch_score = -1
toy_aligner.open_gap_score = -10
toy_aligner.extend_gap_score = -1
print(toy_aligner.align("GATTACA", "GTTCA")[0])
```

Read the printout in three rows. `target` is the first sequence you passed and
`query` is the second. The row between them marks each column: `|` for a match,
`.` for a mismatch, `-` for a gap.

Now change one setting. Gaps get cheaper to open and dearer to extend, and
nothing else moves.

```{python}
toy_aligner.open_gap_score = -2
toy_aligner.extend_gap_score = -2
print(toy_aligner.align("GATTACA", "GTTCA")[0])
```

Different answer, same two sequences.

The first alignment has 4 matches, 1 mismatch, and one gap two columns long.
Score it under the first scoring: 4 − 1 − (10 + 1) leaves it on −8 points. The
second alignment has 5 matches, no mismatches, and two gaps of one column each,
so the second scoring leaves it on 5 − (2 + 2), or 1 point. Now cross them
over. Under the first scoring the second arrangement is worth 5 − 20, or −15.
Under the second scoring the first is worth 4 − 1 − 4, or −1. Each one loses
under the other's rules.

<!-- nlr-allow: 2185 5628 5403 4055 2216 5577 153 225 -->

Neither run consulted a fossil or a phylogeny. Both alignments are correct
answers to the question that was asked, and the questions were different.

## The four numbers you pick, and why two of them are about gaps

Match and mismatch are the easy pair. A match adds, a mismatch subtracts, and
the ratio between them says how much evidence one identical column is worth
against one disagreement.

Gaps take two numbers instead of one. Opening a gap costs a lot and extending
an existing gap costs a little, which is called an
[affine gap penalty]{.term def="A gap costs one price to open and a smaller
price for each extra column, so one long gap is cheaper than several short
ones."}. The reason is biological. One deletion that removes twelve bases is a
single event. Twelve separate one-base deletions are twelve events, and twelve
events are far less likely than one.

Set the open price low and the program will scatter small gaps everywhere. Set
it high and it will accept mismatches instead.

### For proteins the numbers come out of a matrix

DNA has four letters and each is about as good a substitute for the others.
Protein has twenty, and they aren't interchangeable at all. So for protein you
swap the match and mismatch scores for a
[substitution matrix]{.term def="A table giving a score for every pair of amino
acids, built by counting how often each swap turns up in known alignments."}.
It holds one score for each of the 20 × 20 pairs.

Load the one most tools reach for and look at four entries.

```{python}
from Bio.Align import substitution_matrices

blosum62 = substitution_matrices.load("BLOSUM62")
print(blosum62["W"]["W"], blosum62["L"]["L"])
print(blosum62["K"]["R"], blosum62["K"]["W"])
```

Tryptophan against tryptophan is worth far more than leucine against leucine,
because tryptophan is rare and rarely tolerated as anything else. Lysine
against arginine scores positive even though the residues differ, because both
carry a positive charge. Lysine against tryptophan scores negative.

Steven Henikoff and Jorja G. Henikoff built the BLOSUM matrices in 1992 by
counting how often each swap appeared in a collection of protein alignments
they picked. Every number in that table measures one set of proteins rather
than stating a law. Pick a different matrix and you've told the program to
believe something different about how protein changes.

## Global or local, decided by one question

Do you expect the whole of both sequences to correspond? Your answer picks
between the two kinds of alignment.

If the answer is yes, you want a
[global alignment]{.term def="An alignment forced to run end to end through
both sequences, gaps included."}, which forces every base in both sequences
into some column. Saul B. Needleman and Christian D. Wunsch published the
method for that in 1970.

If the answer is no, you want a
[local alignment]{.term def="An alignment reporting only the best-scoring
stretch, free to ignore the rest of both sequences."}. Temple F. Smith and
Michael S. Waterman published that one in 1981.

A short query against a huge database has to be local. In Chapter 6 you sent 28
bases at 948,086,538,397 letters. You asked whether any part of your sequence
resembled any part of anything, and the answer had to be free to come back as
"this stretch, and nothing else."

One gene's coding sequence in two mammals is the other case. You expect them to
correspond over their whole length, so global is the honest choice. That's a
claim, and later in the chapter you'll check it.

## Walkthrough: human BRCA1 against mouse

This chapter uses Biopython, so the install line from Chapter 17 goes at the
top of your notebook.

Load the coding sequences first and confirm the two lengths against what you
recorded in Chapter 5.

```{python}
from Bio import SeqIO

seqs = {}
for record in SeqIO.parse("data/sequences/brca1_cds_five_species.fasta",
                          "fasta"):
    seqs[record.id] = str(record.seq)

human = seqs["human"]
mouse = seqs["mouse"]
print(len(human), len(mouse), len(human) - len(mouse))
```

::: {.check}
The third number is 153, and it's worth holding on to. Divide it by three and
you get 51 codons, which is 1,863 − 1,812, the difference between the two
protein lengths you wrote down in Chapter 5. Two records fetched separately, on
two different pages, agreeing to the base. If your third number isn't 153, you
loaded the wrong two keys.
:::

Now build an aligner with the scores from earlier and run it on the real pair.

```{python}
aligner = PairwiseAligner(mode="global")
aligner.match_score = 1
aligner.mismatch_score = -1
aligner.open_gap_score = -10
aligner.extend_gap_score = -1

alignment = aligner.align(human, mouse)[0]
human_row = alignment[0]
mouse_row = alignment[1]
print(alignment.score, len(human_row))
```

`alignment[0]` is the human sequence written out with its gaps in place, and
`alignment[1]` is the mouse one. Both are ordinary strings and both are 5,628
characters long, because every alignment has the same number of columns in
every row.

Do the subtraction and you have the gap counts already. The human row is 5,628
long and holds 5,592 real bases, so 36 of its columns are gaps. The mouse row
holds 5,439, so 189 of its columns are gaps. And 189 − 36 = 153, the number
from the opening paragraph.

One more thing about that `[0]`. It isn't decoration.

```{python}
print(len(aligner.align(human, mouse)))
```

That's how many arrangements tie for the highest score. Over two quadrillion of
them, all scoring 2185.0, and `[0]` hands you one. Every claim in the rest of
this chapter is a claim about one member of that pile. It is not the true
history of the two genes, and no output anywhere says otherwise.

### Percent identity is two different numbers

[Percent identity]{.term def="The share of alignment columns where both
sequences carry the same base. The denominator varies between programs."} is
the number everybody quotes, and its denominator is a choice.

```{python}
def percent_identity(top, bottom):
    identities = 0
    columns = 0
    for top_base, bottom_base in zip(top, bottom):
        if top_base != "-" and bottom_base != "-":
            columns += 1
            if top_base == bottom_base:
                identities += 1
    return identities, columns, round(100 * identities / columns, 2)


print(percent_identity(human_row, mouse_row))
```

`zip` walks two strings at once and hands you one pair of letters at a time, so
each pass of that loop is one column of the alignment.

4,055 columns hold the same base in both sequences. The function counts only
the 5,403 columns where both rows have a base at all, so it reports 75.05
percent. Divide the same 4,055 by all 5,628 columns instead and you get 72.05
percent. Same alignment, same identities, two answers, and neither is wrong.

### Where the 153 bases went

Gaps come in runs, and the gap prices you set treat a run as one event. Count
the runs rather than the columns.

```{python}
def gap_runs(row):
    runs = []
    length = 0
    for base in row:
        if base == "-":
            length += 1
        elif length > 0:
            runs.append(length)
            length = 0
    if length > 0:
        runs.append(length)
    return runs


human_gaps = gap_runs(human_row)
mouse_gaps = gap_runs(mouse_row)
print(len(human_gaps), sum(human_gaps))
print(len(mouse_gaps), sum(mouse_gaps))
```

`runs.append(length)` sticks `length` on the end of the list `runs`, which is
how you grow a list you started empty. And `elif` means "otherwise, if": it's
tested only when the `if`
above it came out false, so a column that isn't a gap closes whatever run was
in progress.

The first printed line is the human row. 6 runs of gaps, 36 columns between
them, so 6 places where the mouse carries bases the human one doesn't. The
second line is the mouse row: 27 runs, 189 columns, 27 places the other way.
Each run is an
[indel]{.term def="An insertion or a deletion. Which one it is depends on which
sequence you call the original, and an alignment can't tell you."}, and 33
separate events sit between these two genes. The 153 bases are not one block.

Which of the 33 were insertions and which were deletions? Your alignment can't
say. Both sequences are modern, and the ancestor they share isn't in your file.
Chapter 19 brings in more species partly for this reason.

Now sort the run lengths and print them in two halves.

```{python}
all_gaps = sorted(human_gaps + mouse_gaps)
whole_codons = 0
for gap in all_gaps:
    if gap % 3 == 0:
        whole_codons += 1
print(all_gaps[:17])
print(all_gaps[17:])
print(whole_codons, len(all_gaps))
```

`gap % 3` is the remainder after dividing by three, so `gap % 3 == 0` asks
whether a run is a whole number of codons. Every single one of the 33 is. No
run of 1, no run of 2, no run of 4. The shortest is three columns and the
longest is 42, which is 14 codons.

::: {.why}
Chapter 13 had you translate in threes. An indel of one or two bases inside a
coding sequence moves every codon boundary downstream of it. The rest of the
protein then comes out as unrelated amino acids and usually hits an early stop.
That version of the gene is broken, and a broken BRCA1 doesn't get carried down
a lineage. What survives long enough for anyone to sequence it is overwhelmingly
whole codons. You didn't tell the aligner any of this. It fell out of the
letters.
:::

Where along the gene do these 33 events sit? Count the gap columns in each
third of the alignment, with `else` catching whatever the two tests above it
didn't.

```{python}
one_third = len(human_row) / 3
first_third = 0
middle_third = 0
last_third = 0
for column in range(len(human_row)):
    if human_row[column] == "-" or mouse_row[column] == "-":
        if column < one_third:
            first_third += 1
        elif column < 2 * one_third:
            middle_third += 1
        else:
            last_third += 1
print(first_third, middle_third, last_third)
```

All three thirds carry gaps, so the 153 bases are scattered rather than parked
at one end. Add the three counts and you get 24 + 111 + 90 = 225, which is the
36 gap columns in the human row plus the 189 in the mouse row. The first third
holds far fewer than the other two, and one alignment of one pair of species
isn't enough to say why. Write that down and carry it into Chapter 19.

### The number moves when the rules move

Set up the same alignment with none of the four scores specified and see what
Biopython does on its own.

```{python}
default_aligner = PairwiseAligner()
print(default_aligner.match_score, default_aligner.mismatch_score,
      default_aligner.open_gap_score, default_aligner.extend_gap_score)

default_alignment = default_aligner.align(human, mouse)[0]
print(default_alignment.score, len(default_alignment[0]))
print(percent_identity(default_alignment[0], default_alignment[1]))

default_runs = gap_runs(default_alignment[0]) + gap_runs(default_alignment[1])
default_whole_codons = 0
for gap in default_runs:
    if gap % 3 == 0:
        default_whole_codons += 1
print(len(default_runs), default_whole_codons)
```

A mismatch scores zero out of the box, so disagreement is free, and a gap opens
for the same price as it extends. The percent identity that comes back is
77.25, which is higher than the 75.05 you got from the scores this chapter
chose.

::: {.trap}
The default settings give a better-looking percent identity and a worse answer.
The last line says 165 gap runs through the gene instead of 33, and only 14 of
those 165 are whole codons. Nothing errors, nothing warns, and the headline
number goes up. If you report percent identity without reporting the scores you
used, you have reported nothing.
:::

## Two sequences that have nothing to do with each other

Take the mouse sequence, shuffle its bases into random order, and align the
result against human BRCA1. The scrambled string has the same length and the
same base composition as `mouse`, and no shared history with anything.

```{python}
import random

local_aligner = PairwiseAligner(mode="local")
local_aligner.match_score = 1
local_aligner.mismatch_score = -1
local_aligner.open_gap_score = -10
local_aligner.extend_gap_score = -1

local_alignment = local_aligner.align(human, mouse)[0]
local_human = local_alignment[0]
print(local_alignment.score, len(local_human),
      len(local_human) - local_human.count("-"))

random.seed(1)
letters = list(mouse)
random.shuffle(letters)
scrambled = "".join(letters)

junk_alignment = local_aligner.align(human, scrambled)[0]
print(junk_alignment.score, len(junk_alignment[0]))
print(percent_identity(junk_alignment[0], junk_alignment[1]))
print(junk_alignment)
```

`list(mouse)` breaks the string into a list of single characters and
`random.shuffle` reorders that list in place. `random.seed(1)` fixes which
reordering you get, so your numbers match the ones above.

The first line is the check promised earlier. Run human against mouse locally,
where the program may trim as much as it likes, and it keeps 5,577 of the 5,592
human bases in a 5,592-column alignment. Local mode dropped 15 bases, which is
the evidence that global was the right call.
The local score of 2216 beats the global 2185 because local mode can stop
wherever the score is highest.

The rest of the cell is the warning.

::: {.trap}
Alignment always returns something. Two sequences with no relationship still
produce a best arrangement, a score of 15 and a percent identity of 94.12. No
part of that output carries a flag saying the answer is meaningless. The
number looks superb until you notice the alignment is 17 columns long. Length
and coverage are what separate that hit from a real one, which is the same
lesson the E-value taught you in Chapter 7.
:::

:::

Your gap columns in the mouse row minus your gap columns in the human row must
come to exactly 153 columns. That holds for any scoring you pick, because both
sequences are forced end to end and their lengths differ by 153. Then divide by
three, which gives 51 codons, and 1,863 − 1,812 gives the same 51 from the two
protein lengths in Chapter 5. If you get anything but 153, you're in local mode
or you loaded the wrong records.

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'Bio'"}
Python is talking, and it's telling you Biopython isn't in this session. Colab
starts fresh every time, so the install line from Chapter 17 has to run again
at the top of the notebook. Run it, then run your import cell again.
:::

::: {.errfix err="KeyError: 'Human'"}
Python is talking, and the key you asked `seqs` for isn't in it. The ids in
that FASTA file are lowercase: `human`, `chimpanzee`, `mouse`, `dog`,
`chicken`. Print `list(seqs)` to see exactly what you have.
:::

::: {.errfix err="ValueError: invalid mode (expected 'global', 'local', or 'fogsaa'"}
Biopython is talking. That message is copied exactly off the version this page
was built on, unbalanced bracket included, and the words inside the brackets
have changed between Biopython releases. You passed `mode` something it doesn't
recognize. The two words you want are spelled `global` and `local`. There's no
`semiglobal` and no `glocal` here, whatever a paper called it.
:::

::: {.errfix err="The cell has been running for several minutes and nothing has printed"}
Nothing is talking, which is its own signal. A pair of coding sequences this
size aligns in about a second. The work grows with the two lengths multiplied
together, so a pair of whole mRNA records is slower and a chromosome will not
finish while you watch. Interrupt the cell and print the two lengths before you
run it again.
:::
:::
